newsitem.title: USA: Schrager's Mondrian hotel wins big crowds in L.A.
newsitem.headline: Schrager's Mondrian hotel wins big crowds in L.A.

text.p: Ian Schrager is known for attracting fast-lane crowds to his rapidly expanding group of boutique hotels, but the newly re-opened Mondrian on the Sunset Strip may be his fastest success yet.
"It's been like grabbing onto a lightning bolt," Schrager said in a recent interview.

Thirteen years ago Schrager and former business partner, the late Steve Rubell, opened the Morgans, a small hotel in midtown New York that catered to the celebrities and socialites who crowded their landmark nightclub, Studio 54.

Since then his company, Ian Schrager Hotels Inc., has opened two other hotels in New York, the Royalton and Paramount, one in Miami, the Delano, and it is building a hotel in San Francisco. Combined with the Mondrian, those hotels are expected to generate over $50 million in net income annually.
In addition, last week the company announced plans to create a chain of hotels in Europe with Burford Holdings Plc, and separately it is currently four hotels in London.

His success at attracting crowds to his hotels should come as little surprise to people who know of Schrager's reputation for starting businesses that appeal to the fashionably hip. But what may be surprising are his methods for achieving profits because they are based on fairly simple business strategies that contrast directly with his fancy clients. Schrager buys low and sells high, knows what his customers want and sticks closely to his core market.

Schrager acquired the 245-room Mondrian for $17.4 million in 1995. He has spent $15 million over the last 1-1/2 years renovating it from a marble and chrome homage to the 1980's into a light and airy hangout for young celebrities, models, rock stars and people who want to be around them.
The result, since the renovation was finished in December, has been a hotel that is 90 percent booked into the summer and lobby restaurants and bars that are a hub of activity.

Currently, the hottest sector in the lodging industry is the full-service upscale hotel, many of which were built in the 1980's for tax shelter reasons and can now be bought for 70- to 80-percent of their replacement cost.
A new, upscale hotel can cost as much $300,000 a room to build versus up to $200,000 a room to buy, according to Frank Nardozza, national hospitality director at accounting firm KPMG Peat Marwick.
At a total acquisition and renovation cost just over $32 million, Schrager opened the Mondrian for a little over $130,000 per room, meaning he bought low.
But he sells the Mondrian's rooms at a high price, anywhere from $150 per night up to $385 for a suite.

He caters to the same clients who might stay at the nearby Argyle, Chateau Marmont or Sunset Marquis, but he undercuts their room rates 10 percent or more so his customers believe they are getting a good value. And maybe they are.
"People are always going to want to be a part of what's happening," Schrager said.

Schrager knows what his customers want. Currently in Los Angeles, few hotels are as "happening" as the Mondrian. Its nightclub, Sky Bar, is packed on weekend nights with young Hollywood agents, managers, actors and models.
He labels the hotel as part of his unique "alternative" brand that "is all a part of being modern" and "has a point of view and something to say."
Schrager hired French designer Philippe Stark to design a hotel that, Schrager said, blended into its L.A. environment.

The result is a lot of light colors, white drapes, bleached wood floors and clear glass doorways. The lobby is open and breezy and the rooms are oriented toward the floor-to-ceiling windows in order to "bring the outside in."

Finally, Schrager sticks closely to his core market, branding his hotels with his "alternative" touch that is easily recognizable to customers around the world. His next hotels will be in fashionable San Franciso and London.
"I have customers in those cities every year," he said, adding he wouldn't open a hotel in a city just to be there, rather he must go where his core clients are.
